I reproduced every number on the ANSUR II CSV with my own script (n 4,082; official equation mean 24.10, SD 5.68, P5 15.24, P50 24.03, P95 33.53, min 8.19, max 48.63; FFMI P50 20.81; S P50 21.35; Taylor equation mean 26.61, P5 17.26, P95 36.47). The numbers are right. The 'consistency check' is wrong. The official and Taylor equations have the same weight coefficient, so for any man the gap is −0.08 + 0.07 × waist in inches: 2.2 points at 32 in, 2.4 at 36 in, 2.7 at 40 in. Taylor's DXA cohort has almost the same body size as ANSUR II (85.9 vs 85.5 kg; BMI 27.6 vs 27.7). Taylor's own 1-site equation has a male bias of only −0.39, which implies a mean abdomen of about 90.9 cm. On that cohort the official equation would give about 21.5%, about 2.8 points below the measured 24.3%. My inference assumes bias = predicted − DXA, which the −4.79 AR bias confirms. ANSUR II's navel waist averages 94.1 cm, about 3 cm more at the same weight, perhaps from a different measuring protocol. So the 24.1 vs 24.3 'match' is two offsets of about 3 points cancelling, not a validation. Taylor's DXA-fitted equation puts the ANSUR mean at 26.6%. The honest statement is a mean of about 24–27%, median S 20.6–21.4 and median FFMI 20.1–20.8. The headline still stands: the median man scores about 21, not 24. At the median height (1.755 m) and weight (84.6 kg), S = 24 needs 14.8% fat. Scripts: scratchpad/research/fat-check/scripts/ansur_check.py and ansur_vs_taylor.py.

On Taylor's representative DXA cohort the official equation reads about 2.8 points below DXA (derived; see the ansur2 check), and Taylor's DXA-fitted equation gives ANSUR 2.4–2.7 points more for every man. The group range 15–34 should span both equations (P5 15.2 to P95 36.5). The working median should be about 24–27%, not a single 24. 'S proportional to (1 − fat): 15 vs 34% changes S by about 22%' is right relative to the lean end (0.66/0.85).

Mostly sound and well labelled. Overstatements: (1) Rec 2 centres everyday builds on the official equation and says 'S ≈ 21, not 24'. The conclusion holds (20.6–21.4), but the body-fat centre should span both equations (24–27%). (2) Rec 3 calls 13% 'Kouri's non-user mean'. It is the overall approximate mean from secondary sources. (3) Rec 5's 'max reported about 30–32' is not supported by any fact in this research. Its only basis is Helms' secondary remark on Kouri ('some users reached about 32') in the existing key, so cite it as such or drop it. (4) Rec 5 states Bhasin's +2.4 FFMI without noting it was in GnRH-suppressed men and that the training status is unconfirmed. (5) Rec 4 and the summary call DXA contest-day natural values 'lab-grade ... 4.5–6.3%'. Only Barakat (n = 1) is confirmed DXA on contest day. (6) The summary says 'Users' average real-world dose was 973 mg/week'. That is one cohort of 51 middle-aged long-term US users, self-reported.

missing:
- Different DXA machines give different numbers. NHANES used a Hologic QDR 4500A with NCHS's 5% lean-to-fat correction (1999–2004) and APEX 4.0 software (2011–18). Taylor, Bosch and Kraemer used GE Lunar. Barakat used a Hologic. 'DXA' body fat is not strictly comparable across chart groups, and the research never mentions this. At minimum, say so on the page.
- No published accuracy figure for the official AD 2023-11 men's equation. Only Taylor's slightly different equation has an RMSE and bias, and on Taylor's cohort the official equation implies about −2.8 points (derived). The USARIEM 2,690-soldier study is 'pending publication' per Army.mil. Neither AD 2023-11 nor ALARACT 046/2023 was fetched.
- ANSUR II's navel waist (mean 94.1 cm) is about 3 cm larger than the abdomen implied for Taylor's soldiers at the same weight. The cause (measuring protocol vs real difference) is unresolved and should be stated as a limitation.
- The body-fat method is unconfirmed for Rossow 2013 and Mitchell 2018 (both abstracts are silent) and for Bhasin 2001 (also unconfirmed: no-training design). Heights are missing for Barakat, Mitchell, Rossow and Yu, so no FFMI can be computed for them.
- NHANES 2011–18 DXA men's percentiles: Liu's appendix table 6 and the public NHANES DXA files could give current percentiles to replace or check the 1999–2004 table. Not fetched.
- No lab (DXA or 4C) body fat for any Olympia-level pro, for super-heavyweight weightlifters, or for the named strongmen Hall and Bjornsson (acknowledged by the researcher). Kouri 1995's full text (the 13% and the 'about 32' user maximum) is still secondary.
- Sources for a few asides are missing: Raymond 2018 (BIA vs DXA in football players), and the claim that stage diuretics lower FFM water rather than fat.
verdict:
Transcription is accurate. I re-fetched 16 full texts or PDFs (NCHS sr11_250, the Army IG PDF, Liu, Taylor, Barakat, Robinson, Rosaci, Giakoni, Baggish, Hudson, Bulut, Buhl, Kaufman, Yu, Bosch, Martinez-Mireles) and 17 abstracts, plus the Army.mil article. Every quoted table cell I checked matches. All derived FFMI, S, Coleman and Kondo numbers recompute, and the ANSUR II statistics reproduce exactly.

What needs fixing:

(1) The ANSUR II check is wrong. The official equation's 24.1% only coincidentally matches the 24.3% DXA soldier mean. On Taylor's own DXA cohort, which is the same body size, the official equation would read about 2.8 points low, and Taylor's DXA-fitted equation gives ANSUR 26.6%. Everyday men should therefore carry about 24–27% median fat (range about 15–37%). The headline survives: median S is about 21 (20.6–21.4), not 24.

(2) Small number errors:
- Robinson's end body fat is 6.7–6.8%, not 7.2%.
- Buhl's 61 current-user men is stated in the paper, not inferred.
- Taylor's Table 1 gives n = 1259.
- Barakat's ultrasound-vs-DXA gap is 1.4–2.7 points.
- The S sensitivity bands are asymmetric: +2/−4% for natural stage, +1/−3% for enhanced stage.
- The strongman-range rationale does not match its numbers.

(3) Evidence overstated:
- The 'DXA' label for Rossow and Mitchell is unconfirmed, so lab-grade contest-day natural data are one subject (Barakat 6.3%).
- Kouri's 13% is an overall secondary figure, not a non-user mean.
- 'Max about 30–32' for steroid users is unsupported here.
- Bhasin 2001's 'no training' and 'DXA' are unconfirmed.
- Withers' 'probably enhanced' is an inference and must be labelled as one.

Statuses are otherwise appropriate. The magazine-relayed Shaw value stays 'reported', and the secondary review stays 'reported'.
